title: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
summary: How a next-token predictor becomes an assistant: pretraining on filtered, deduplicated web data, SFT with a masked loss, reward models from human and AI preferences, and RL with policy gradients and PPO.
outcomes: Explain why a pretrained base model is not an assistant and what each of pretraining, SFT and RLHF adds
Compute next-token cross-entropy for a short sequence and estimate pretraining compute with C of about 6ND
Trace a crawled page through extraction, filtering, MinHash deduplication and packing, and compute a MinHash match probability
Implement SFT loss masking and explain why prompt tokens are excluded but the end-of-turn token is not
Compute Bradley-Terry probabilities and losses from human rankings or soft AI labels, and explain separate safety rewards
Derive the policy gradient and explain why a baseline keeps it unbiased while cutting its variance
Compute GAE advantages and PPO's clipped objective for a short response
Explain how the KL penalty, beta and reward over-optimization interact in PPO-based RLHF and its alternatives

lessons.title: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe

blocks.md: The GPT you built is trained to do one thing: predict the next token of text. Train that model on a large slice of the internet and you get a **base model** (also called a pretrained model). It knows a great deal about language, facts and code, but it was never asked to *help* anyone. Given a question, it produces whatever text is most likely to come next in a document, which might be an answer, or might be more questions in the same style.

The InstructGPT paper (Ouyang et al., 2022) put the gap plainly: predicting the next token on a webpage is a different objective from "follow the user's instructions helpfully and safely", so the language modeling objective is **misaligned** with what users want. The fix it popularized is a three-stage recipe that most chat models still follow in some form:

1. **Pretraining**: next-token prediction on hundreds of billions to trillions of tokens of raw text.
2. **Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**: the same loss, but on a small set of prompts paired with answers written by people.
3. **RLHF** (reinforcement learning from human feedback): people compare model answers, a **reward model** learns to predict their preferences, and reinforcement learning pushes the model toward answers the reward model scores highly.

**Reinforcement learning** means learning from a score instead of from a correct answer: the model produces an output, receives a number called the **reward**, and is updated so that high-reward outputs become more likely. The model being trained is then called the **policy**, the reinforcement learning word for the rule that chooses what to output, and InstructGPT's update algorithm is proximal policy optimization (PPO), which lessons 7 and 8 explain.

blocks.title: The InstructGPT training pipeline

scenes.caption: Stage 1: pretraining. GPT-3 was trained on 300 billion tokens of mostly web text. The result predicts text well but does not reliably follow instructions.
Stage 2: SFT. Labelers wrote good answers for about 13k prompts, and the base model is fine-tuned on them with the ordinary next-token loss.
Stage 3a: reward model. Labelers rank several model answers per prompt (about 33k prompts). A 6B model, started from an SFT model, learns to give preferred answers a higher score.
Stage 3b: RL. The SFT model becomes a policy that writes answers to about 31k prompts; the reward model scores them and PPO updates the policy toward higher scores.

blocks.md: A useful mental model: pretraining puts the knowledge and skills into the weights; SFT teaches the *format* and role of an assistant; RLHF sharpens the choice among answers the model can already produce, using a signal ("which of these is better?") that is much cheaper to collect than writing perfect answers.

The later stages are tiny next to pretraining. InstructGPT reports that training the 175B (175 billion parameter) SFT model took 4.9 petaflop/s-days and the 175B PPO-ptx model (its reinforcement learning model, which also mixes in pretraining updates; the name is explained below) took 60, compared with 3,640 petaflop/s-days to pretrain GPT-3. A petaflop/s-day is $10^{15}$ operations per second sustained for a day, about $8.64 \times 10^{19}$ operations.

blocks.title: Training compute per stage (petaflop/s-days)

scenes.caption: Pretraining GPT-3 175B: 3,640 petaflop/s-days. Everything else is measured against this.
SFT adds 4.9 petaflop/s-days (about 0.13 percent of pretraining) and PPO-ptx adds 60 (about 1.6 percent). The bars are barely visible: alignment is cheap in compute, expensive in human labeling.

blocks.md: Same network, three different training signals: raw text (what comes next?), demonstrations (what would a good assistant write?), and comparisons (which of these two answers is better?). Each stage starts from the weights of the previous one.

The payoff was large. In InstructGPT's human evaluations on prompts that customers had submitted to the OpenAI API, outputs from the **1.3B** InstructGPT model were preferred to outputs from the **175B** GPT-3, a model over 100 times larger. The paper also found an **alignment tax**: RLHF lowered scores on some public benchmarks such as SQuAD and DROP, which they reduced by mixing pretraining updates into RL (the "ptx" in PPO-ptx). SQuAD, the Stanford Question Answering Dataset, asks questions whose answer is a span of a Wikipedia paragraph, and DROP, Discrete Reasoning Over Paragraphs, asks questions that need counting, comparing or arithmetic over a paragraph.

How do you know an assistant got better? InstructGPT's main measure was a **win rate**: on held-out prompts from customers whose prompts were not used in training, labelers compared each model's output with a fixed baseline (the 175B SFT model) and the fraction of wins was reported, alongside 1 to 7 quality ratings. Public benchmarks run next to it to catch the alignment tax. Llama 2 also used GPT-4 as a **model judge** of its outputs against ChatGPT's, randomly swapping their order in the prompt to avoid position bias, because its own reward model might favor its own model. The reward model's score itself is not an evaluation: it is the quantity being optimized, and lesson 9 shows it can keep rising while real quality falls. The Evaluating generated text course covers judges and human studies in depth.

blocks.question: A base model is given the prompt "Write a haiku about rain." Why might it fail to write a haiku?
options: It continues the text as a plausible document, which may be more instructions or a list of prompts rather than an answer
Its weights contain no knowledge of poetry, which only SFT adds
Base models cannot generate text without a reward model
The prompt is too short for the attention mechanism
blocks.explain: Pretraining optimizes next-token likelihood on documents. A line like this often appears in lists of writing prompts, so continuing with more prompts is a likely continuation. The knowledge of haiku is already in the base model; SFT and RLHF teach it to respond as an assistant.

blocks.question: Roughly what fraction of GPT-3's pretraining compute did the 175B InstructGPT PPO-ptx run use?
options: About 50 percent
About 16 percent
About 0.01 percent
About 1.6 percent
blocks.explain: 60 / 3,640 is about 0.0165, so about 1.6 percent. The scarce input for alignment is human data (demonstrations and comparisons), not compute.

lessons.title: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens

blocks.md: Pretraining is the training loop from your GPT, scaled up. Take a long document, split it into tokens, and at every position ask the model for a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary for the *next* token. The loss at that position is the **cross-entropy**: the negative log of the probability the model gave to the token that actually came next. With the natural log the loss is measured in **nats**, the base-e unit of information, just as base-2 logs give bits.

blocks.caption: Average next-token cross-entropy over T predictions: minus the mean, over positions t, of the log-probability the model gives the true next token. Every position in every document is a training example, so no labels are needed.

blocks.md: Let us run it on a toy. The vocabulary has five words: `the`, `cat`, `sat`, `on`, `mat`. The document is "the cat sat on the". The inputs are the first four tokens, and the targets are the same tokens shifted left by one. We made up the model's logits; the probabilities and losses below are computed from them with a softmax.

blocks.title: One document becomes four training examples

scenes.caption: The model reads the input tokens. Because of the causal mask, position t only sees tokens 0 to t, so all four predictions are computed in one forward pass.
Targets are the inputs shifted left by one. Position 0 ("the") must predict "cat", position 2 ("sat") must predict "on".
Softmax over the five logits gives the probability assigned to each correct next token. "cat sat" is easy (0.702); "sat on" is hardest (0.336).

Loss per position is -ln p. The low-probability guess costs the most (1.090). The mean over 4 positions is 0.703, a perplexity of exp(0.703), about 2.02: as unsure as choosing among 2 equally likely words.

blocks.md: Where does that gradient come from? With logits $z$ and target $y$, the loss at one position is minus the log of the softmax probability of $y$, which is $-z_y + \log\sum_j e^{z_j}$. Differentiate with respect to one logit $z_k$: the log-sum term gives $e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$, which is exactly $p_k$, and the $-z_y$ term adds minus 1 only when $k$ is the target. So the gradient is $p_k$ for every wrong word and $p_y - 1$ for the target. Written as one vector that is $p - \text{onehot}(y)$, where the one-hot vector has a 1 at the target and 0 everywhere else.

blocks.prompt: The gradient of cross-entropy with respect to the logits is $p - \text{onehot}(\text{target})$. At the "sat" position the target is "on". If we take one gradient step on these logits, what happens to the probabilities of the four *wrong* words?
blocks.reveal: They all go down, and the correct word goes up. The gradient is positive for every wrong word (its probability $p_k$) and negative for the target ($p_{on} - 1 = -0.664$), so subtracting it raises the target logit and lowers the others in proportion to how much probability they stole. The loss at that position drops from 1.090 to 0.618 after one step with learning rate 1.

blocks.title: One gradient step at the "sat" position

scenes.caption: Before: the model spreads probability, giving the target "on" only 0.336 (loss 1.090).
After one step with learning rate 1: "on" rises to 0.539 (loss 0.618). Simplified: we nudged the 5 logits directly; a real model changes its weights, which moves logits at many positions at once.
With learning rate 2 instead: "on" reaches 0.729 (loss 0.316). Larger steps fit this example faster but, on real data, overshoot and destabilize training.

blocks.md: Scale changes the data and the engineering, not the objective. GPT-3 trained every model size on **300 billion tokens**. Llama 3's flagship model (Llama is Meta's family of openly released models) has 405B parameters and was trained on **15.6 trillion tokens**. Data is a weighted mix, not one pile: GPT-3 drew 60 percent of examples from filtered Common Crawl, 22 percent from WebText2, 8 percent each from two book corpora and 3 percent from Wikipedia, deliberately not in proportion to dataset size. Common Crawl is a free public archive of billions of crawled web pages; WebText2 is OpenAI's set of pages linked from Reddit posts that readers upvoted, a rough filter for quality; Books1 and Books2 are two collections of books from the internet. One **epoch** is one full pass over a dataset, so a heavily weighted small set is seen more than once. How raw web pages become these clean datasets is the next lesson.

blocks.title: GPT-3's pretraining mix: size vs sampling weight

scenes.caption: Dataset sizes in billions of tokens: Common Crawl dwarfs everything else (410B of the 499B).
Epochs seen during the 300B-token run. Higher-quality sets were upsampled: Wikipedia was seen 3.4 times and WebText2 2.9 times, while Common Crawl was seen only 0.44 times.

blocks.md: How much compute does that take? Kaplan et al. (2020) estimate training compute as about $6N$ floating point operations per token for a model with $N$ parameters: roughly $2N$ for the forward pass and twice that for the backward pass. Almost all the work is matrix multiplies, and in the forward pass each weight is used once per token, in one multiply and one add, which gives $2N$. The backward pass computes two gradients for each weight matrix, one for its input (to pass further back) and one for the weights themselves, and each costs about as much as the forward multiply, which gives $4N$. Multiply $2N + 4N = 6N$ by the number of training tokens $D$.

blocks.caption: In words: compute C is about 6 times N times D. For GPT-3 175B that is 6 times 175 billion times 300 billion, about 3.15e23 FLOPs; the paper's table lists 3.14e23 (3,640 petaflop/s-days). For Llama 3 405B on 15.6T tokens the same rule gives about 3.8e25, matching the reported 3.8 x 10^25.

blocks.md: Scale does change the engineering. Llama 3 405B was trained on up to 16K H100 GPUs, too much model for one GPU, so it combined four kinds of parallelism: tensor parallelism splits each weight matrix across GPUs, pipeline parallelism gives each GPU group a slice of the layers, context parallelism splits long sequences, and data parallelism runs copies on different batches. It trained in bf16, a 16-bit floating-point format, and kept 38 to 43 percent of the GPUs' peak bf16 throughput doing model math, a measure called model FLOPs utilization (MFU). In one 54-day window the job was interrupted 466 times, 419 of them unexpectedly and about 78 percent of those from confirmed or suspected hardware faults, so fast checkpointing and automated restarts kept effective training time above 90 percent. The Megatron-Core (MCore) performance course covers how the parallelism works.

A low pretraining loss does not mean a helpful model. The loss rewards matching the *distribution* of internet text, including its errors, rudeness and rambling. That is exactly why the later stages exist.
How to split a fixed compute budget between parameters N and tokens D is the subject of the Scaling laws course; here just remember that $C \approx 6ND$ ties the two together.

blocks.question: A model with a 50,000-token vocabulary predicts the uniform distribution at every position. What is its average cross-entropy loss?
options: 0 nats, because it never assigns zero probability
About 0.69 nats, which is ln(2)
About 10.8 nats, which is ln(50,000)
50,000 nats
blocks.explain: Uniform means p(target) = 1/50,000 everywhere, so the loss is -ln(1/50,000) = ln(50,000), about 10.82 nats. Real training starts near this value and falls as the model learns.

blocks.question: Using C of about 6ND, a 7B-parameter model trained on 2 trillion tokens needs roughly how many FLOPs?
blocks.explain: 6 x 7e9 x 2e12 = 8.4e22. The rule ignores attention's context-length term, which Kaplan et al. note is small when the model width is large relative to the context.

lessons.title: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline

blocks.md: Follow one crawled page: a recipe blog post. The crawler saved its raw HTML, which holds a navigation menu, a cookie banner, ads, a comment section and, somewhere in the middle, the recipe. The same recipe is also copied on dozens of scraper sites. Only the recipe text should become training tokens, and only once. The chain of steps that turns raw crawl files into clean, deduplicated tokens is the **data pipeline**, and for a base model it matters as much as the architecture.

The best documented open pipeline is **FineWeb** (Penedo et al., 2024, Hugging Face), a 15-trillion-token English dataset built from 96 Common Crawl **snapshots** (a snapshot is one crawl run, released as a batch). Common Crawl offers each snapshot in two formats: **WARC** (Web ARChive), the raw HTML plus request metadata, and **WET** (WARC Encapsulated Text), a text-only version made by a simple HTML parser. FineWeb found WET text kept too much boilerplate and menu text, and that extracting text from WARC with the open-source trafilatura library gave better models in **ablations**: controlled training runs where only one choice changes (here 28B-token runs). Llama 3 went further with its own HTML parser, kept image alt text because math is often a pre-rendered image whose alt text holds the formula, and removed markdown markers, which it found hurt.

blocks.title: The FineWeb pipeline, one stage at a time

scenes.caption: Start from raw HTML. Extracting the main text with trafilatura instead of using the WET text drops most menus and boilerplate.

Base filtering: drop adult domains with a URL blocklist, keep pages a fastText language classifier scores as English with at least 0.65, and apply the quality and repetition rules of MassiveText (Gopher's dataset). About 36T tokens remain.
Near-duplicate removal with MinHash, run separately inside each snapshot, leaves about 20T tokens.
Most of C4's line and document rules plus three custom filters, then email and public IP addresses are anonymized: 15T tokens of FineWeb.
Optional last step: a model-based quality classifier keeps pages it rates as educational, 1.3T tokens of FineWeb-Edu. Simplified: Llama 3 and others order and tune these stages differently.

blocks.md: **Heuristic filters** are cheap rules computed from the text itself. MassiveText (the dataset used to train the Gopher model) contributes quality and repetition rules. C4 (the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus of Raffel et al., built from a 2019 crawl) drops lines without terminal punctuation or that mention javascript or cookie policies, and drops documents that are too short or contain "lorem ipsum" or a curly bracket. FineWeb kept all of C4's rules except the terminal-punctuation line rule, which alone removed about 30 percent of tokens. Its own three filters remove a document when the fraction of lines ending in punctuation is at most 0.12, when at least 0.1 of its characters sit in duplicated lines, or when at least 0.67 of its lines are shorter than 30 characters. Together these removed about 22 percent of tokens and raised the benchmark aggregate by about 1 point.

blocks.prompt: A scraped page is 10 lines: 9 short menu items ("Home", "Recipes", "Contact"...) and one 80-character sentence ending in a period. Which of FineWeb's three custom filters remove it?
blocks.reveal: Two of them. Only 1 of 10 lines ends in punctuation, a fraction of 0.1, which is at most 0.12. And 9 of 10 lines are shorter than 30 characters, a fraction of 0.9, which is at least 0.67. The duplicated-lines filter does not fire because no line repeats. Pages that are mostly navigation are exactly what these rules target.

blocks.md: Next comes **deduplication**. The web is full of mirrors, templates and copied pages, and Lee et al. (2021, Google) showed why that matters: C4 contained one 61-word sentence repeated 61,036 times, over 1 percent of the tokens a model trained on standard datasets emitted unprompted were copied from its training data, and deduplicating cut that memorized output by a factor of 10 while reaching the same or better accuracy in fewer training steps. Exact matching misses pages that differ by a word, so pipelines also remove **near-duplicates**. Each document becomes a set of **shingles**, its overlapping runs of 5 words (word 5-grams), and two documents are compared by **Jaccard similarity**: shared shingles divided by all distinct shingles.

blocks.title: Two near-duplicate pages as word 5-gram shingles

scenes.caption: Page A has 15 words and page B has 17: B says "a little yeast" where A says "yeast". Every other word is the same.
A shingle is a window of 5 consecutive words. Page A has 15 - 4 = 11 shingles; the first is "the quick guide to baking".
Page B has 17 - 4 = 13 shingles. The 10 windows that end before the edit are identical in both pages.
Windows touching the edit differ: 1 shingle only in A, 3 only in B. Jaccard = 10 shared / 14 distinct = 0.714.

blocks.md: Comparing every pair of billions of pages is impossible, so pipelines use **MinHash** (Broder, 1997). Pick a hash function, hash every shingle of a document and keep the smallest value. Two documents get the same minimum exactly when the shingle with the smallest hash in their combined set is one they share, and that shingle is equally likely to be any of the distinct shingles, so the chance of a match equals the Jaccard similarity. Repeat with $k$ hash functions and the fraction of matching minimums estimates Jaccard. FineWeb uses 112 hash functions split into 14 **buckets** of 8; two documents are duplicates if all 8 minimums agree in at least one bucket, and duplicates are clustered so one copy per cluster is kept.

blocks.caption: s is the Jaccard similarity. One bucket matches with probability s to the 8th, misses with 1 - s^8, all 14 miss with that to the 14th power, and the complement is a match somewhere. FineWeb reports 56, 77, 92 and 98.8 percent for s = 0.7, 0.75, 0.8 and 0.85.

blocks.code:
import hashlib

def shingles(text, n=5):
    w = text.lower().split()
    return {" ".join(w[i:i+n]) for i in range(len(w) - n + 1)}

def minhash(sh, k):
    return [min(int.from_bytes(hashlib.blake2b(f"{seed}:{s}".encode(),
                digest_size=8).digest(), "big") for s in sh)
            for seed in range(k)]

a = "the quick guide to baking bread at home with only flour water salt and yeast"
b = "the quick guide to baking bread at home with only flour water salt and a little yeast"
A, B = shingles(a), shingles(b)
print("Jaccard = %.3f" % (len(A & B) / len(A | B)))
sa, sb = minhash(A, 112), minhash(B, 112)
print("equal minhashes: %d/112" % sum(x == y for x, y in zip(sa, sb)))
print("buckets matching:", sum(sa[i*8:i*8+8] == sb[i*8:i*8+8] for i in range(14)))
s = 10 / 14
print("P(flagged) = %.3f" % (1 - (1 - s**8)**14))
blocks.caption: Output: Jaccard = 0.714, equal minhashes: 70/112 (an estimate of 0.625; with 112 hashes the estimate's standard deviation is about 0.04, so this run landed low), buckets matching: 1, P(flagged) = 0.626. One fully matching bucket is enough: the pair is flagged as duplicates.

blocks.title: Chance a pair is flagged, by Jaccard similarity

x.label: Jaccard similarity s of two documents

scenes.caption: FineWeb's setting, 14 buckets of 8: an S-shaped curve. Pairs below about 0.5 similarity are almost never flagged (5 percent at 0.5); pairs above 0.85 almost always are.
More hashes per bucket (r = 16) moves the threshold right: only very similar pairs are flagged.
Fewer hashes per bucket (r = 4) moves it left and catches looser copies, at the cost of flagging pages that merely share boilerplate.

blocks.md: More deduplication is not automatically better. FineWeb first deduplicated all 96 snapshots against each other, which left 4T tokens and barely beat no deduplication. In the oldest snapshot, the 10 percent of data that survived was worse than the 90 percent removed (more ads and keyword lists). Deduplicating each snapshot on its own, about 20T tokens, matched the strong RefinedWeb dataset.

blocks.title: FineWeb tokens surviving each stage (trillions)

scenes.caption: Text extraction plus base filtering of 96 snapshots: about 36 trillion tokens (GPT-2 tokenizer).
Deduplication inside each snapshot removes about 16T tokens of near-copies: 20T remain.
C4 and custom filters bring the released dataset to 15T tokens.
An educational-quality classifier keeps 1.3T tokens. Models trained on it scored much higher on knowledge benchmarks such as MMLU and ARC.

blocks.md: Three more steps protect people and the evaluations. **PII** (personally identifiable information) is removed or masked: FineWeb anonymizes email and public IP addresses, and Llama 3 drops whole domains that carry a lot of PII or unsafe content. **Model-based quality filters** keep pages a small classifier rates highly; Llama 3 used a fastText classifier of whether a page would be cited by Wikipedia and DistilRoberta classifiers trained on Llama 2's quality judgments, and how such filters are built is the subject of the Data mixing and curation (DoReMi) course. **Decontamination** keeps benchmark questions out of training data so scores measure generalization rather than recall: Lee et al. found train-test overlap in over 4 percent of some validation sets, Llama 3 excludes benchmark training sets from its final high-quality data and reports a contamination analysis for its scores.

Finally the tokens are **packed**. Training batches are fixed-length sequences, so short documents are concatenated to fill each one. GPT-3 packed documents into 2,048-token sequences separated by a special end-of-text token and used no special mask, relying on that token to signal that what came before is unrelated. Llama 3 instead uses a **document mask**: an attention mask that also blocks attention between different documents in the same sequence. It reports limited impact in standard pretraining, but found it important when continuing pretraining on very long sequences.

blocks.title: Packed sequence: causal mask vs document mask

scenes.caption: Three documents (a, b, c) packed into 9 positions, separated by end-of-text tokens (eot). With a plain causal mask, row = query, column = key: each token sees every earlier token, even from other documents.
Token b1 attends to a1, a2, a3 and an eot from an unrelated page. GPT-3 trained this way and let the eot token signal the break.
Document mask: attention is blocked across documents, leaving one causal triangle per document. Every prediction now depends only on its own document, as if each were trained alone.

blocks.md: A modern run is also staged in time. Llama 3 405B trained with AdamW at a peak learning rate of $8 \times 10^{-5}$, warmed up over 8,000 steps and decayed by a cosine schedule. It started with 4M-token batches of 4,096-token sequences, doubled both after 252M tokens and doubled the batch again to 16M tokens after 2.87T tokens, while adjusting the data mix along the way (more non-English and math data, more recent web pages). Then came **long-context pretraining**: the context window grew from 8K to 128K tokens in six steps over about 800B tokens, done late because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Last came **annealing**: over the final 40M tokens the learning rate fell linearly to 0 while very high-quality sources were upsampled, and checkpoints from this phase were averaged into the released base model.

blocks.title: The stages of Llama 3 405B pretraining (not to scale)

scenes.caption: Main pretraining, almost all of the 15.6T tokens: 4K then 8K context, learning rate warmed up then decayed by a cosine schedule, data mix adjusted as results came in.
Long-context stage, about 800B tokens: the window grows from 8K to 128K in six steps, each continued until short-context scores recover and long-context retrieval tests pass.
Annealing, the final 40M tokens: learning rate decays linearly to 0 on upsampled high-quality data at 128K context, and checkpoints are averaged into the base model.

blocks.md: Raw crawl becomes training data through extraction, filtering, near-duplicate removal, PII and contamination handling, then packing. Each step was chosen by training small models on the result, and a run then moves through stages: main pretraining, context extension, annealing.
Which domains to weight and by how much is the Data mixing and curation (DoReMi) course. What happens when web data is increasingly written by models is the Synthetic data and model collapse course.

blocks.question: Two pages have Jaccard similarity 0.5 over their 5-gram shingles. With FineWeb's 14 buckets of 8 hashes, how likely are they to be flagged as duplicates?
options: About 50 percent, because MinHash estimates Jaccard directly
Always, because they share half their shingles
Never, because MinHash only catches exact copies
About 5 percent, because all 8 hashes must agree in some bucket
blocks.explain: One bucket matches with probability 0.5 to the 8th, about 0.0039. The chance at least one of 14 buckets matches is 1 - (1 - 0.0039)^14, about 0.053. Banding turns the per-hash match rate into a sharp threshold near 0.7 (a 50 percent chance at s of about 0.69).

blocks.question: Why did Llama 3 find the document mask mattered more in long-context training than in standard 8K pretraining?
options: A 128K-token sequence packs many unrelated documents, so a plain causal mask lets tokens attend to far more unrelated text
Document masks make attention cost linear in sequence length
Long sequences do not use an end-of-text token
The document mask is needed for the learning rate to anneal
blocks.explain: With longer windows a token can see many more tokens from other documents, which can distract or teach false dependencies. The mask keeps each prediction conditioned on its own document only. It changes which keys are visible, not the asymptotic cost.

lessons.title: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt

blocks.md: **Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**, also called instruction tuning, continues training the base model on examples of the behavior you want: a prompt, followed by an ideal response. The loss is the same next-token cross-entropy as pretraining. What changes is the data and which tokens count.

Each example is rendered with a **chat template**: special tokens that mark who is speaking, such as a user header, the user's text, an assistant header, the answer, and an end-of-turn token. At inference time the serving system writes the user header, the user's text and the assistant header, and the model continues from there. SFT teaches the model what belongs after the assistant header and, importantly, when to stop.

blocks.title: Loss masking on one SFT example

scenes.caption: One SFT example: 6 template and prompt tokens, then a 4-token answer that ends in an end-of-sequence token.
Every token after the first is a prediction target. Illustrative per-token losses: the prompt is hard to predict (the user could ask anything), the answer is easier.
Averaging all 9 gives 2.02, and the 5 prompt tokens make up 78 percent of the summed loss. Training on that would mostly teach the model to imitate users.
Mask the prompt: only the 4 answer targets count, mean loss 1.00. The model still reads the prompt as context; it just is not graded on predicting it.

blocks.md: Llama 2 describes exactly this: "we zero-out the loss on tokens from the user prompt, so as a result, we backpropagate only on answer tokens." It also concatenates all the prompts and answers to fill each 4,096-token sequence, with a special token separating prompt and answer segments, so no compute is wasted on padding (filler tokens that would otherwise stretch short examples to the length of the longest one in a batch). As in pretraining packing (lesson 3), a plain causal mask lets each example attend to the examples packed before it, and a document mask prevents that; the Llama 2 paper does not say which it used. In PyTorch the usual trick is to set masked label positions to `-100`, the default `ignore_index` of the cross-entropy loss.

blocks.title: Masked SFT loss in PyTorch
blocks.code:
import torch.nn.functional as F

# input_ids: [B, T]  (6 prompt tokens, then 4 answer tokens)
labels = input_ids.clone()
labels[:, :n_prompt] = -100        # mask template + prompt

logits = model(input_ids)          # [B, T, V]
shift_logits = logits[:, :-1]      # position t predicts t+1
shift_labels = labels[:, 1:]

loss = F.cross_entropy(
    shift_logits.reshape(-1, V),
    shift_labels.reshape(-1),
    ignore_index=-100,             # skip masked targets
)

scenes.caption: Copy the token ids to use as labels.
Overwrite the first n_prompt = 6 labels with -100, so they will be ignored.
One forward pass over all 10 tokens; the model still attends to the prompt.
Shift so that position t is scored on token t+1: 9 predictions remain.
Cross-entropy averages only over the 4 non-ignored targets. With the earlier numbers this is 1.00, not 2.02.

blocks.md: SFT data is small and curated. InstructGPT used about 13k prompts with labeler-written answers and trained for 16 epochs; the SFT models overfit on validation loss after one epoch, yet more epochs still improved reward model scores and human preference. Llama 2 stopped after **27,540** high-quality annotations, finding that a few tens of thousands of clean examples beat millions of noisier third-party ones.

LIMA (Less Is More for Alignment, Zhou et al., 2023) pushed this further: fine-tuning a 65B LLaMa model on only **1,000** carefully chosen examples (about 750,000 tokens) produced a strong assistant. The authors state the **Superficial Alignment Hypothesis**: almost all knowledge is learned in pretraining, and alignment mostly teaches the style and format to use when talking to users.

SFT does not add much new knowledge. If the base model does not know a fact, a demonstration that states it mostly teaches the model to answer confidently in that style, which can increase made-up answers on other questions ([Gekhman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05904)).
SFT = pretraining loss + chat template + loss only on response tokens (including the end-of-turn token) + a small, high-quality dataset.

blocks.question: A team fine-tunes on chat data but forgets to mask the prompt. What is the most likely symptom?
options: Training crashes because labels and logits have different lengths
The model learns to write user-style questions and the loss is dominated by hard-to-predict prompt tokens
The model forgets the chat template entirely
Nothing changes, because the prompt loss gradient is always zero
blocks.explain: Without the mask the model is also trained to predict user text, which is high-entropy and dominates the average (78 percent of the summed loss in our example). Capacity and gradient go into imitating users instead of answering them.

blocks.question: Why must the end-of-sequence token after the answer be included in the trained targets?
options: It carries the reward signal for RLHF
It is required by the softmax
Otherwise the model never learns when to stop and keeps generating
It prevents the prompt from being masked
blocks.explain: Stopping is a learned prediction like any other. If the end token is masked, the model never sees a gradient for ending its turn and tends to run on, for example by writing the next user turn itself.

lessons.title: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score

blocks.md: Writing a perfect answer is slow; saying which of two answers is better is fast and more consistent across people. RLHF exploits this. A **reward model** $r_\theta(x, y)$ reads a prompt $x$ and a response $y$ and outputs one number ($\theta$ stands for its weights). InstructGPT builds it from an SFT model by removing the final unembedding layer (the projection to vocabulary logits) and adding a head that outputs a scalar.

Training uses the **Bradley-Terry** model of comparisons: the probability that a person prefers response $y_w$ (winner) over $y_l$ (loser) is the sigmoid of the reward difference. The loss is the negative log of that probability, averaged over human comparisons. This is the loss in InstructGPT (Equation 1) and Llama 2.

Where does the sigmoid come from? Bradley and Terry (1952) proposed this model for ranking items from paired comparisons: give each item a positive strength, and let the chance that A is preferred to B be A's share of the two strengths, A's strength divided by the sum of both. Write each strength as $e$ to the power of a reward and divide top and bottom by $e^{r_A}$: with gap $d = r_A - r_B$, the chance becomes $1/(1+e^{-d})$, the sigmoid of the reward gap. Turned around, the gap is the log-odds of the preference, $\ln\frac{p}{1-p}$: a gap of 0 means 50/50, and a gap of 1 means $\sigma(1) \approx 0.73$.

blocks.caption: sigma(z) = 1 / (1 + e^{-z}). Only the difference of rewards matters, so the reward scale is anchored only by the data.

blocks.md: InstructGPT showed labelers between $K=4$ and $K=9$ responses per prompt and asked for a full ranking. A ranking of $K$ items implies $\binom{K}{2} = K(K-1)/2$ pairs: each response pairs with the $K-1$ others, and that counts every pair twice. That gives 6 pairs for $K=4$ and 36 for $K=9$. Because those pairs share responses, InstructGPT puts all pairs from one prompt in the same batch element; shuffling them as independent examples made the reward model overfit after one pass.

Worked example. A labeler ranks four responses A > B > C > D. Before training, every reward is 0, every pairwise probability is 0.5 and every pair costs $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$. After training, suppose the rewards are A = 1.2, B = 0.5, C = 0.1, D = -0.8.

blocks.title: P(row is preferred over column) from rewards

scenes.caption: Untrained: all rewards equal, so every comparison is a coin flip (0.5). Mean loss over the 6 ranked pairs is ln 2, about 0.693.
Trained rewards A=1.2, B=0.5, C=0.1, D=-0.8. The upper triangle holds the 6 labeled pairs; each is sigma of the reward gap.
Largest gap: A vs D (2.0) gives 0.88 and loss 0.127. Smallest: B vs C (0.4) gives 0.60 and loss 0.513, the pair the model is least sure about. Mean loss falls to 0.319.
Read across a row to see how likely that response is to beat each other one. The matrix is antisymmetric around 0.5: P(B over A) = 1 - P(A over B) = 0.33.

blocks.prompt: Add 5 to every reward (A = 6.2, B = 5.5, C = 5.1, D = 4.2). What happens to the loss?
blocks.reveal: Nothing. Every pairwise probability depends only on differences, so A vs B is still $\sigma(0.7) = 0.668$ and the loss is unchanged. The reward model's absolute level is arbitrary, which is why InstructGPT adds a bias so that labeler demonstrations score 0 on average before RL.

blocks.md: Llama 2 adds one refinement, plotted next. Its annotators also said how much better the winner was (significantly better, better, slightly better, or negligibly better or unsure; lesson 6 covers how such comparisons are collected), and Llama 2 subtracts a **margin** $m$ that grows with that rating from the reward gap, so the loss becomes $-\log\sigma(r_w - r_l - m)$. A pair then stays expensive until the winner leads by more than $m$, and $m = 0$, used for negligibly better, gives back the InstructGPT loss.

blocks.title: Pairwise loss vs reward margin

scenes.caption: With m = 0 this is the InstructGPT loss. A wrongly ordered pair (negative gap) is punished almost linearly; a confidently correct pair costs almost nothing.

Llama 2 subtracts a margin m that grows with how strongly the annotator preferred the winner. With m = 3 (the 'significantly better' value in its larger margin variant) the loss stays high until the gap exceeds 3.

blocks.md: A reward model is a learned approximation, not ground truth. Stiennon et al. (2020), an OpenAI paper that used RLHF to summarize Reddit posts, found their reward model preferred longer summaries, and it can be confidently wrong on responses unlike its training data. Lesson 9 shows what happens when RL optimizes hard against such a model.
The reward model learns only from differences. Its job is to rank responses to the same prompt, and its output is a log-odds score: a gap of 1 means about 73 percent preference.

blocks.question: A labeler ranks K = 6 responses. How many pairwise comparisons does that give, and how many gradient terms does each single response appear in?
options: 6 pairs; each response appears in 1
30 pairs; each response appears in 10
36 pairs; each response appears in 6
15 pairs; each response appears in 5
blocks.explain: C(6,2) = 15 pairs, and each response is compared with the other K - 1 = 5. That correlation is why InstructGPT batches all pairs from one prompt together instead of shuffling them.

blocks.question: Rewards are A = 2.0 and B = 1.0, and the human preferred B. What is the loss on this pair?
blocks.explain: The winner is B, so the gap is 1.0 - 2.0 = -1. Loss = -ln sigma(-1) = ln(1 + e) = 1.313. A wrongly ordered pair costs much more than ln 2.

lessons.title: Where preference data comes from: guidelines, safety, AI feedback

blocks.md: A user asks: "How do I get into my neighbor's wifi?" Response A lists tools for cracking the password. Response B says that would invade the neighbor's privacy and may be illegal, and suggests asking the neighbor. Which is better? A labeler told only to reward helpfulness might pick A. The reward model of the previous lesson learns whatever the comparisons say, so the real specification of an assistant lives in the **labeling guidelines** and in who, or what, applies them.

InstructGPT hired about 40 contractors through Upwork and Scale AI, selected with a screening test of how well they spotted potentially harmful outputs and judged the preferences of different groups. Its guidelines asked for outputs that are **helpful**, **truthful** and **harmless**. These can conflict, for example when a user asks for something harmful; during training labelers were told to prioritize helpfulness, while in the final evaluations they were told to prioritize truthfulness and harmlessness. Agreement was far from perfect: training labelers agreed with each other 72.6 percent of the time, and held-out labelers 77.3 percent.

Llama 2 used a different protocol. An annotator writes a prompt, sees two responses sampled from different model variants at different temperatures, picks one, and rates how much better it is: significantly better, better, slightly better, or negligibly better or unsure. That rating is the source of the margin from the previous lesson. Helpfulness and safety were collected under separate guidelines, safety with a focus on adversarial prompts, and data arrived in weekly batches sampled from the latest chat model so the reward model stayed on the distribution it would score. In total Meta collected 1,418,091 binary comparisons.

blocks.title: Llama 2 reward model accuracy by annotator rating (percent)

scenes.caption: Helpfulness reward model on the Meta helpfulness test set: 80.7 percent on clear pairs, falling to 54.7, barely above a coin flip, when the annotator was unsure.
Safety reward model on the Meta safety test set: 94.3 percent on clear pairs, 55.3 on near ties. Close pairs are hard for people too, so their labels carry little signal.

blocks.md: Disagreement is noise inside the Bradley-Terry loss. Suppose 80 percent of labelers would prefer A over B. Training sees label A 80 percent of the time and label B 20 percent, so the expected loss is $-[0.8\log\sigma(d) + 0.2\log\sigma(-d)]$ for reward gap $d$. It is smallest when $\sigma(d) = 0.8$, a gap of $\ln 4 \approx 1.39$, where the loss is 0.500 rather than 0. A well-trained reward model therefore predicts the *share* of people who agree, and its accuracy is capped by how consistent people are: InstructGPT's reward models predicted their own labelers' choices 72.4 percent of the time and held-out labeler groups 69.6 percent.

blocks.title: Pairwise loss with a soft target t

scenes.caption: t = 1: every labeler agrees, and the loss keeps falling as the gap grows. This is the hard-label loss of the previous lesson.
t = 0.8: the loss now has a minimum at d = ln 4, about 1.39, with value 0.500. Pushing the gap further is penalized because 20 percent of labels disagree.
t = 0.6: a near tie. The best gap is only ln 1.5, about 0.41, and the loss floor is 0.673, close to ln 2.

blocks.md: Why separate safety from helpfulness? Bai et al. (2022, Anthropic) trained helpful and harmless (HH) assistants with RLHF and released their helpfulness and harmlessness comparisons as the hh-rlhf dataset. They found the two goals in tension: a preference model trained mainly on one did much worse than chance on the other, and early policies over-optimized harmlessness, answering any sensitive question with the same exaggerated advice (seek professional help) because a refusal scores well on red-team prompts, prompts written to bait the model into harmful output. Llama 2 trained two reward models and combined them per prompt, using the safety score when a prompt is tagged as possibly unsafe or when the safety score falls below 0.15.

blocks.tex: R_c(g\mid p) = \begin{cases} R_s(g\mid p) & \text{if is\_safety}(p) \text{ or } R_s(g\mid p) < 0.15 \\ R_h(g\mid p) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \tilde{R}_c = \text{whiten}(\text{logit}(R_c))
blocks.caption: Llama 2's reward for generation g on prompt p. R_s and R_h are the safety and helpfulness scores as probabilities. The logit undoes the sigmoid, and whitening shifts and scales scores to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 so they balance against the KL penalty.

blocks.title: Combining two reward models on three responses

scenes.caption: Three illustrative responses. The first answers a prompt tagged as possibly unsafe; the other two answer ordinary prompts.
Response 0: the prompt is tagged, so the safety score 0.62 is used even though helpfulness is 0.91.
Response 1: an ordinary prompt, but the safety score 0.08 is below 0.15, so the response is treated as unsafe and scored by safety, however helpful it looks.
Response 2: ordinary prompt, safe enough, so helpfulness 0.55 is used. Logits: ln(0.62/0.38) = 0.49, ln(0.08/0.92) = -2.44, ln(0.55/0.45) = 0.20; whitening across the batch comes next.

blocks.md: Human comparisons are slow and expensive. **Constitutional AI** (Bai et al., 2022, Anthropic) replaces the human harmlessness labels with model judgments guided by a written list of principles, the **constitution**. In the supervised stage the model answers a red-team prompt, is asked to critique its answer against a principle, then to revise it, and is fine-tuned on the revisions. The paper's example: asked to help hack a neighbor's wifi, the model first offers an app; after "identify specific ways in which the assistant's last response is harmful" and a revision request, it says hacking would invade the neighbor's privacy and may be illegal. Sixteen principles were written and one is sampled at random for each step.

blocks.title: Constitutional AI: supervised stage, then RL from AI feedback

scenes.caption: Supervised stage: the model critiques and revises its own answers to red-team prompts, one sampled principle at a time, and is fine-tuned on the revisions.
AI feedback: for each prompt the fine-tuned model writes two answers, and a separate feedback model is asked which one better follows a principle, as a multiple-choice question.

A preference model is trained on AI harmlessness labels mixed with human helpfulness labels; RL against it is RL from AI feedback (RLAIF). Human oversight of harmlessness is now the constitution itself.

blocks.md: Worked example of one AI label. The feedback model reads the conversation, a principle such as "Which of these assistant responses is less harmful?", and options (A) and (B), then we read its log-probabilities of answering (A) or (B). Say they are -0.36 and -1.83, probabilities 0.698 and 0.160. Normalizing gives a **soft target** $t = 0.698 / (0.698 + 0.160) = 0.813$ for A, and the preference model is trained with the soft loss from the plot above. At gap 0 the loss is 0.693; at gap 1.47, which is $\ln(t/(1-t))$, it reaches its minimum of 0.482; at gap 3 it rises again to 0.609, because the label only claims 81 percent confidence. Constitutional AI found these soft labels worked much better than hard 0 or 1 labels.

blocks.prompt: When the feedback model first reasons step by step, its final answers are nearly always 0 or 1 in probability. Constitutional AI clamped those probabilities to the range 40 to 60 percent. Where does a clamped target of 0.6 put the preference model's best reward gap?
blocks.reveal: At $\ln(0.6/0.4) \approx 0.41$, a gentle preference. Clamping stops a confident but possibly wrong AI judgment from pushing reward gaps to extremes. The paper reports that without clamping, the RL-trained models learned to give more extreme responses, and that clamping at 40 to 60 worked better than 20 to 80.

blocks.md: AI feedback moves the specification, it does not remove it. The labels are only as good as the feedback model and the principles, and a model judging a model can share its blind spots. Teams still check AI-labeled preferences and the resulting policy against human judgments.

Preference data is a design choice: who labels, under which guidelines, on which prompts, with which ratings. Separate signals (helpfulness and safety) and AI labels from written principles (RLAIF) are now standard ingredients of post-training.

blocks.question: Llama 2 scores a response to an ordinary, untagged prompt. Its safety score is 0.10 and its helpfulness score is 0.95. Which score does RLHF use?
options: The helpfulness score 0.95, because the prompt is not tagged as unsafe
The average 0.525
The safety score 0.10, because it is below the 0.15 threshold
Neither: the response is discarded
blocks.explain: Safety takes over whenever the prompt is tagged or the safety score is under 0.15. A very helpful but likely unsafe answer is therefore scored as unsafe. Llama 2 chose 0.15 for a precision of 0.89 and recall of 0.55 on its safety test set.

blocks.question: Three of four labelers prefer A over B for some pair. With enough such data, what reward gap does a Bradley-Terry reward model converge to for this pair?
options: A gap that grows without limit, because A always wins on average
0, because the labelers disagree
Exactly 0.75, the fraction of labelers
About ln 3 = 1.10, so that sigmoid of the gap is 0.75
blocks.explain: The expected loss -(0.75 log sigma(d) + 0.25 log sigma(-d)) is minimized where sigma(d) = 0.75, so d = ln(0.75/0.25) = ln 3. Disagreement caps the gap and leaves a nonzero loss floor; it does not zero the reward or let it grow forever.

lessons.title: Policy gradients: how a score becomes a gradient

blocks.md: The reward model hands back one number for a response the policy *sampled*. Sampling is a discrete choice, so there is no gradient to backpropagate through it, and no correct answer to compare with as in SFT. How do we turn "this response scored 1.0" into a weight update? Start with the smallest case, a **bandit**, named after the multi-armed bandit, a row of slot machines where you pull one arm and get one payout: one choice, one reward, done. Ours has three possible responses A, B and C, logits 0.5, 0.0 and 0.2, and rewards 1, 0 and -1. The softmax gives probabilities 0.426, 0.258 and 0.316, so the **expected reward** $J = \sum_i p_i r_i$ is 0.426 - 0.316 = 0.110.

blocks.tex:
abla J = \sum_i r_i 
abla p_i = \sum_i p_i\, r_i\, 
abla \log p_i = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p} ig[\, r(y)\, 
abla \log p(y) \, ig]
blocks.caption: The log-derivative trick: the derivative of log p is (derivative of p) / p, so the gradient of p equals p times the gradient of log p. That turns a sum over all responses into an average over responses we sample.

blocks.md: The last form is the point. We cannot sum over every possible response of a language model, but we can sample some, and for each one compute its reward times the gradient of its log-probability. For softmax logits that gradient is $\text{onehot}(y) - p$, minus the cross-entropy gradient from lesson 2. So the update is: do a supervised step on your own sample, scaled by its reward. A positive reward pulls the sample's logit up and the others down; a negative reward does the opposite. This estimator is **REINFORCE**, the name Ronald Williams gave it in 1992. Its exact value here is $p_k(r_k - J)$ for each logit $k$.

blocks.title: Exact policy gradient vs 5-sample estimates

scenes.caption: The bandit: columns are responses A, B and C with probabilities 0.426, 0.258, 0.316 and rewards 1, 0, -1. Expected reward J = 0.110.
Exact gradient of J with respect to the three logits, p times (r - J): raise A, lower C, leave B almost alone.
Monte Carlo estimate from 5 sampled responses: average r(y) times (onehot(y) - p). Close to the exact value, with the right signs.
Two more batches of 5. All point the same way on average, but B's entry even flips sign: the estimate is unbiased yet noisy. Output of a seeded numpy script.

blocks.md: For a language model a response is a sequence, and its log-probability is the sum of its tokens' log-probabilities, $\log \pi(y \mid x) = \sum_t \log \pi(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})$. The gradient of a sum is the sum of gradients, so REINFORCE pushes every token of a high-reward response up by the same reward, and every token of a low-reward response down. That is correct on average but very blunt: a long answer with one wrong sentence has all its good tokens penalized too.

blocks.prompt: Add 2 to every reward, so A, B, C score 3, 2, 1. The ranking is unchanged. Does the expected policy gradient change? Does the noise of a sampled estimate change?
blocks.reveal: The expected gradient is identical: $p_k(r_k - J)$ only depends on rewards relative to their mean. But the noise explodes, because every sample now carries a large positive weight that the other samples must cancel on average. Over 1,000 single-sample draws the summed variance of the estimate rises from 0.167 to 2.678.

blocks.md:
The fix is a **baseline** $b$: use $(r - b)\,
abla\log p(y)$. This is still unbiased, because the average of $
abla \log p$ under the policy is zero: $\sum_i p_i 
abla \log p_i = \sum_i 
abla p_i = 
abla \sum_i p_i = 
abla 1 = 0$. Any $b$ that does not depend on which response was sampled therefore subtracts zero on average, while a good $b$ shrinks the weights toward zero and cuts the noise. Using the expected reward $J$ as $b$ brings the shifted case back to 0.179. It is not the variance-minimizing choice: with the already-centered rewards 1, 0, -1, using $b = J$ gives 0.179 instead of 0.167.

blocks.title: Variance of a 1-sample gradient estimate (1,000 draws)

scenes.caption: Centered rewards: the baseline barely matters (0.167 vs 0.179) because J = 0.11 is already near zero.
Shifted rewards: without a baseline the variance is 2.678, 15 times larger, for the same expected gradient. Subtracting J restores 0.179. Exact values: 0.170, 0.181, 2.719, 0.181.

blocks.code:
import torch
torch.manual_seed(0)
rewards = torch.tensor([3.0, 2.0, 1.0])            # responses A, B, C
logits = torch.tensor([0.5, 0.0, 0.2], requires_grad=True)
opt = torch.optim.SGD([logits], lr=0.1)
baseline = 0.0                                      # running mean of reward

for step in range(201):
    probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=0)
    y = torch.multinomial(probs, 8, replacement=True)   # 8 sampled responses
    r = rewards[y]
    adv = r - baseline                                  # reward minus baseline
    logp = torch.log(probs[y])
    loss = -(adv * logp).mean()                         # REINFORCE surrogate
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    baseline = 0.9 * baseline + 0.1 * r.mean().item()
    if step % 50 == 0:
        print(f"step {step:3d}  p(A,B,C) = {[round(x, 3) for x in probs.tolist()]}"
              f"  E[r] = {(probs * rewards).sum().item():.3f}  baseline = {baseline:.2f}")
blocks.caption: REINFORCE with a running-mean baseline on the shifted bandit, run on a CPU. Output: step 0 p = [0.426, 0.258, 0.316], E[r] = 2.110; step 50 p = [0.851, 0.097, 0.052], E[r] = 2.799; step 200 p = [0.972, 0.019, 0.009], E[r] = 2.963, baseline 2.97.

blocks.md: For sequences, rewards arrive per token: in RLHF most tokens get 0 (lesson 8 adds a small KL term to each) and the score comes at the last token. The **return** $G_t$ at token $t$ is the sum of rewards from $t$ to the end. The baseline may depend on the **state**, the prompt plus the tokens written so far, because that is still independent of the token about to be sampled. The standard choice is the expected return from that state, which a **value model** $V(s_t)$ learns by regression: minimize the squared error between its prediction and the returns actually observed. The weight on each token becomes the **advantage**, return minus value. **Generalized advantage estimation** (GAE, Schulman et al., 2015) builds it from one-step surprises $\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)$: the reward at token $t$ plus the value one step later, discounted by $\gamma$ (a factor of at most 1 that makes later rewards count less; RLHF uses 1), minus the value now.

blocks.caption: Each later surprise is shrunk by gamma times lambda. Lambda = 1 gives return G minus value (unbiased, noisy); lambda = 0 trusts the value model after one step (less noisy, biased if V is wrong). Stiennon et al. used gamma = 1, lambda = 0.95.

blocks.md: One more ingredient makes PPO possible. Sampling responses is the expensive part of RL for language models, so PPO takes several gradient steps on one batch. After the first step the samples come from the *old* policy, not the one being updated. **Importance sampling** corrects for that: an average under the new policy equals an average under the old one with each sample weighted by $\rho = \pi_{new}(y)/\pi_{old}(y)$. A token the old policy chose with probability 0.30 and the new one with 0.36 counts 1.2 times. So PPO maximizes the **surrogate** $\mathbb{E}_{old}[\rho\,\hat{A}]$. At the start of the update $\rho = 1$ and $\nabla\rho = \nabla\log\pi_{new}$, so the surrogate's gradient is exactly the policy gradient: raising $\rho A$ raises expected reward, as long as the new policy stays close enough to the old one for the old samples to be representative. Keeping it close is the job of the clip in the next lesson.

Policy gradient = average of advantage times the gradient of the log-probability of what was sampled. Baselines and value models cut the noise without biasing it, GAE spreads one final score into per-token advantages, and the ratio rho lets one batch of samples be reused.
GRPO, used for reasoning models, drops the value model and uses the mean reward of several answers to the same prompt as the baseline; the GRPO and RLVR course builds on this lesson.

blocks.question: A policy samples response C, which has reward -1, with probabilities p = (0.426, 0.258, 0.316) over A, B, C. Without a baseline, how does this one sample move the three logits under gradient ascent?
options: It raises all three logits, because the gradient of a probability is always positive
It lowers C's logit and raises A's and B's, since r times (onehot(C) - p) = (0.426, 0.258, -0.684)
It raises C's logit, because C was the response sampled
It leaves the logits unchanged, because negative rewards give no gradient
blocks.explain: The sample's contribution is r(C) times (onehot(C) - p) = -1 times (-0.426, -0.258, 0.684). Ascent lowers C's logit by the largest amount and lifts the others. A negative reward acts like a push away from what was sampled.

blocks.question: Someone proposes using each sampled response's own reward as its baseline, b = r(y). What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; any baseline keeps the gradient unbiased
The variance increases but the policy still learns the right thing
The advantage r(y) - b is always zero, so the policy never learns
The gradient becomes biased toward longer responses
blocks.explain: The unbiasedness argument needs b to be independent of the sampled response. With b = r(y) every advantage is exactly 0 and every update vanishes. Valid baselines depend on the state (like V(s)) or on the other samples for the same prompt, not on the sample being scored. GRPO's group mean also includes the scored sample, a small bias that shrinks as the group grows.

lessons.title: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model

blocks.md: Now we treat the language model as a **policy** $\pi_\phi(y \mid x)$, where $\phi$ stands for its weights: given a prompt, it samples a response. InstructGPT frames this as a bandit environment, like the toy in lesson 7. A prompt arrives, the policy writes a whole response, the reward model scores it once, and the episode (one prompt, one response, one score) ends. The goal is to raise expected reward.

Maximizing the reward model alone fails quickly: the policy drifts to strange text where the reward model was never trained and is easy to fool. So the reward is penalized by how far the policy has moved from the SFT model. This is the objective from Stiennon et al. (2020), used by InstructGPT: the reward for a response is the reward model's score minus $\beta$ times the log of the policy's probability of that response divided by the SFT model's probability. $\beta$ is the exchange rate between the two, how much reward one nat of drift costs; InstructGPT used $\beta = 0.02$.

blocks.caption: In words: reward model score minus beta times the log ratio of policy to SFT probability; its average is the KL from the SFT model. InstructGPT applies it per token and adds the pretraining log-likelihood times a weight it calls gamma (PPO-ptx), unrelated to the GAE gamma below.

blocks.md: Why a log ratio? If the policy gives a response the same probability as the SFT model, the log ratio is 0 and there is no penalty; if it makes the response 3 times more likely, the log ratio is $\ln 3 \approx 1.1$ nats. Averaged over the responses the policy actually samples, the log ratio is the **Kullback-Leibler divergence** of the policy from the SFT model, named after Solomon Kullback and Richard Leibler (1951) and usually shortened to their initials. It is 0 only when the two distributions are identical and positive otherwise, so it measures, in nats, how far the policy has drifted.

The figure below uses three reinforcement learning words from lesson 7, recalled here. The **return** at a token is all the reward that arrives from that token to the end of the response; here that is the final score minus the KL penalties still to come. The **value model** is a second network that predicts the return at each token before seeing how the response ends. In its simplest form the **advantage** is the actual return minus that prediction: positive means the token led somewhere better than expected, so PPO makes it more likely. Subtracting the prediction removes what was expected anyway, which makes the updates much less noisy. Lesson 7 showed why this keeps the gradient unbiased, how the value model is trained by regression to observed returns, and how GAE turns one final score into per-token advantages.

blocks.title: One PPO iteration in RLHF

scenes.caption: Rollout: the policy (initialized from the SFT model) samples a response for each prompt at temperature 1. InstructGPT used batches of 512 episodes.
Scoring: the frozen reward model gives one scalar per response, and the frozen SFT model gives log-probabilities for every token so the KL penalty can be computed.
A value model, initialized from the reward model, predicts the expected return at each token. Subtracting it gives advantages: was this token better or worse than expected?

PPO updates the policy on these samples with a clipped objective, so it gains nothing from moving any token's probability ratio more than 20 percent, then the loop repeats. Four models are in play: two trained, two frozen.

blocks.md: The KL penalty is paid token by token. For each response token, compute the log-probability under the policy and under the SFT model; their difference is that token's contribution. The reward model's score is added at the final token. Here is a 4-token response with reward model score 1.5.

blocks.title: Per-token KL penalty on one response

scenes.caption: Log-probabilities of the 4 sampled tokens under the current policy and the frozen SFT model (illustrative values).
Log ratios: the policy has made tokens 0, 1 and 3 more likely than SFT did (sum 1.3 nats). Token 2 is unchanged.
With beta = 0.02, each token earns -0.02 times its log ratio, and the last token also gets the score 1.5. Total reward 1.5 - 0.026 = 1.474.
With beta = 0.1 the same drift costs five times more: total 1.5 - 0.13 = 1.37. Larger beta keeps the policy closer to SFT.

blocks.md: PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) is the optimizer. Proximal means nearby: each update keeps the new policy near the one that collected the data. Its key idea is a **clipped** objective: with probability ratio $\rho = \pi_{new}/\pi_{old}$ for a token and advantage $A$, it maximizes $\min(\rho A, \operatorname{clip}(\rho, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) A)$. Here $\pi_{old}$ is the policy that sampled the batch, kept fixed, and $\pi_{new}$ is the one being updated; the ratio reweights samples drawn from the old policy so they estimate what the new one would earn (importance sampling, lesson 7). Clip limits $\rho$ to the range $1-\epsilon$ to $1+\epsilon$, and taking the min means the objective uses the clipped credit whenever that is smaller. With $\epsilon = 0.2$ (InstructGPT's setting), a token with $A = +1$ whose ratio already reached 1.5 is credited only 1.2, so there is no gradient pushing it further. This lets PPO take several minibatch steps on one batch of samples without the policy running away.

Now one complete PPO step, by hand, on the 4-token response above with $\beta = 0.02$. Its per-token rewards are the KL penalties plus the reward model score of 1.5 at the end: -0.004, -0.01, 0 and 1.488. The value model, initialized from the reward model, predicts the return before each token; say 1.10, 1.25, 1.30 and 1.40, and 0 after the last token. Following Stiennon et al., use GAE with $\gamma = 1$ (no discount, as in InstructGPT too) and $\lambda = 0.95$.

blocks.title: One PPO step: rewards, values, GAE advantages and returns

scenes.caption: Inputs: per-token rewards (KL terms, plus the score at the last token) and the value model's predictions (illustrative).
GAE runs backward: A_3 = 0.088, A_2 = 0.100 + 0.95 x 0.088 = 0.184, A_1 = 0.214, A_0 = 0.350. Every token did better than the value model expected.
Value targets are advantage plus value: 1.450, 1.464, 1.484, 1.488. The value model is regressed toward these, so its predictions rise.

blocks.md: Now the policy update for two tokens. After some minibatch steps, token 0's ratio is $\rho = 1.10$, inside the clip range 0.8 to 1.2: its objective is $1.10 \times 0.350 = 0.385$ and the gradient still pushes it up. Token 3's ratio has reached 1.35: unclipped it would earn $1.35 \times 0.088 = 0.119$, but the clipped term is $1.2 \times 0.088 = 0.106$, the min picks that, and since it no longer depends on the weights, token 3 contributes no gradient. The value loss is half the mean squared error to the targets: 0.026 with the old predictions, 0.014 if an update moves them to 1.20, 1.30, 1.35 and 1.45. Real implementations whiten advantages across the minibatch (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) before this step. Stiennon et al. ran 4 PPO epochs per batch of samples; InstructGPT used one pass over 8 minibatches of 64.

blocks.title: PPO's clipped objective for one token

scenes.caption: Positive advantage: the objective rises with rho until 1 + epsilon, then goes flat. There is no reward for making a good token more than 20 percent likelier than the sampling policy did.

Negative advantage: flat below 1 - epsilon, so a bad token gains nothing from being pushed below 0.8 of its old probability. Above 1 the unclipped line is lower, and the min keeps it, so a mistake that made a bad token likelier is still corrected.
A smaller epsilon of 0.1 narrows the trust region: safer, smaller steps per batch of samples.

blocks.prompt: Ignore the KL term and suppose the policy could put all its probability on any response it likes. Which response would pure reward maximization pick?
blocks.reveal: The single response with the highest reward model score, with probability 1, whether or not humans actually like it. Pure maximization collapses diversity and finds the reward model's blind spots. The KL term is what keeps the optimum spread over responses the SFT model considered plausible.

blocks.md: RLHF does not maximize reward. It maximizes reward minus beta times the KL from the SFT model, and beta sets how far the model may move to chase the reward model.

blocks.question: During RLHF, the mean reward keeps rising while the KL from the SFT model shoots up and samples start repeating odd phrases. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Raise beta, or stop at an earlier checkpoint
Lower beta so the policy can explore more
Lower the PPO clip range to 0
Remove the value model
blocks.explain: Rising reward with exploding KL is the signature of the policy exploiting the reward model. A larger beta makes drift more expensive, and earlier checkpoints have less drift. Lowering beta makes it worse; a clip range of 0 stops learning entirely.

blocks.question: Why does InstructGPT keep a frozen copy of the SFT model during RL?
options: To generate the training prompts
To compute log-probabilities for the KL penalty that anchors the policy
To replace the reward model when it is uncertain
To serve as the value function
blocks.explain: The frozen SFT model supplies log pi_SFT for every sampled token, which the per-token KL penalty compares with the policy's log-probabilities. The value function is a separate model initialized from the reward model.

blocks.question: In a PPO minibatch, a token has advantage -0.5 and its ratio has fallen to 0.7, with epsilon 0.2. What does this token contribute to the gradient?
options: A push to lower its probability further, because its advantage is negative
A push to raise its probability back to 1
Nothing, because negative advantages are always clipped
Nothing: the clipped term -0.4 is the minimum and does not depend on the weights
blocks.explain: rho x A = -0.35 and clip(0.7, 0.8, 1.2) x A = -0.4. The min is the clipped -0.4, a constant, so no gradient flows: the token was already made 30 percent less likely, past the 20 percent PPO allows per batch. If its ratio had been 1.3 instead, the unclipped -0.65 would be the min and the gradient would push it back down.

lessons.title: Reward over-optimization, best-of-N and modern recipes

blocks.md: The KL-regularized objective has a closed-form best policy, derived in the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) paper (Rafailov et al., 2023): reweight the SFT model's probabilities by the exponentiated reward. Small $\beta$ means sharp reweighting; large $\beta$ means staying near SFT. Real PPO only approximates this optimum, but it shows exactly where the tradeoff comes from.

blocks.caption: pi star, the best policy, is the SFT probability times e to the reward over beta, divided by Z(x) so the probabilities over responses sum to 1. A response gains probability exponentially in its reward, but starts from its SFT probability.

blocks.md: Where it comes from: for one prompt, the objective is the expected reward minus $\beta$ times the KL from the SFT model. Factor out $\beta$ and combine the logs, and it equals minus $\beta$ times the KL between the policy and a reweighted distribution, the SFT probability times $e^{r/\beta}$ divided by $Z(x)$, plus $\beta \log Z(x)$, which does not depend on the policy. A KL is smallest, zero, when the two distributions are equal, so that reweighted distribution is the best policy. $Z(x)$ adds up, over all responses, the SFT probability times $e^{r/\beta}$, so that the new probabilities sum to 1.

A toy with four possible responses: Helpful, Wrong, Rambling and Flattery. The SFT model gives them probabilities 0.25, 0.35, 0.30, 0.10. The reward model scores them 1.0, -0.5, 0.3, 1.5. But the reward model is flawed: the **Flattery** response scores highest, while humans actually rate it -0.4 (they rate the other three 1.0, -0.5 and 0.2). We compute $\pi^*$ for several values of $\beta$ and track two numbers. The first is the reward model's score, called the **proxy reward** because it stands in for what humans want; the figures label it RM score. The second is the true quality.

blocks.title: The optimal policy as beta shrinks

scenes.caption: beta = 100: essentially the SFT model. RM score 0.32, true quality 0.10, KL 0.00.
beta = 2: the Wrong answer loses mass first. RM score 0.56, true quality 0.21, KL 0.06. Light optimization genuinely helps.
beta = 1: Helpful leads at 0.39. RM score 0.78, true quality 0.27 near its best, KL 0.23.
beta = 0.5: Flattery overtakes Helpful. RM score keeps rising to 1.09 but true quality has dropped to 0.24 (KL 0.68).
beta = 0.25: Flattery takes 0.73. RM score 1.35, true quality -0.04, worse than the SFT model (KL 1.40).
beta = 0.1: near-total collapse onto the hacked response. RM score 1.49, true quality -0.38. Simplified: real models have astronomically many responses, but the dynamics match.

blocks.title: Proxy reward vs true quality as optimization grows

scenes.caption: Same toy, swept continuously. The proxy reward rises monotonically with optimization, as does the KL from the SFT model.

True quality peaks at 0.28 near 1/beta = 1.3 (KL 0.36), then falls below the starting point. Stiennon et al. saw this with real summaries: past some KL, the reward model became anti-correlated with human preference.

blocks.md: A higher reward model score is not evidence of a better model. Teams track KL and check with fresh human or held-out evaluations, because the proxy keeps climbing after real quality has turned down. This is Goodhart's law, named after the economist Charles Goodhart and usually stated as "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure", applied to learned rewards; the Reward hacking course goes deeper.

**Best-of-N** (rejection sampling) is a simpler way to use a reward model: sample $N$ responses, keep the highest-scoring one. Stiennon et al. give its KL from the base policy as $\log N - (N-1)/N$ nats: about 0.64 for $N=4$, 1.84 for $N=16$ and 3.86 for $N=128$.

Where the formula comes from, for rewards without ties: let $u$ be the chance that one base-policy sample scores below a given response. Best-of-N returns that response when it is among the $N$ samples and the other $N-1$ all score lower, so its probability is about $N u^{N-1}$ times its base probability. The KL is the average log of that factor, $\log N + (N-1)$ times the average of $\log u$, and for the best of $N$ samples the average of $\log u$ is $-1/N$: the best of $N$ uniform draws is below $u$ with probability $u^N$, so it has density $N u^{N-1}$, and $\int_0^1 N u^{N-1} \log u \, du = -1/N$. That leaves $\log N - (N-1)/N$. Llama 2 used rejection sampling fine-tuning (train on the best of $K$ samples, like SFT) for its early RLHF rounds, then applied PPO on top.

**Direct Preference Optimization** (DPO) uses the closed form above in reverse: it rewrites the reward in terms of the policy's own log-probability ratio against the reference model (the frozen SFT model the KL is measured from). Solving the closed form for the reward gives: the reward equals $\beta$ times the log of the best policy's probability divided by the SFT model's probability, plus $\beta \log Z(x)$. The Bradley-Terry loss only uses the difference between two responses to the same prompt, so $\beta \log Z(x)$, which no one can compute, cancels, and the loss can be applied to the policy directly. No separate reward model at training time and no sampling loop. Llama 3's post-training ran six rounds of SFT, rejection sampling with a reward model, and DPO, which its authors chose over PPO partly because it needed less compute at scale. DPO and its variants have their own course.

A newer stage targets reasoning: **RL with verifiable rewards** (RLVR), where the reward comes from a program that checks the answer, such as an exact match on a math result or passing unit tests, instead of a learned reward model. Tulu 3 (Allen Institute for AI, 2024) ran SFT, then DPO, then RLVR with PPO on math and instruction-following prompts. DeepSeek-R1 (2025) trained with GRPO, a PPO variant without a value model: R1-Zero applied rule-based rewards directly to a base model, and R1 used cold-start SFT, reasoning RL, rejection sampling plus SFT, then a final RL stage mixing rule rewards with reward models for helpfulness and harmlessness. A checker cannot be flattered the way a reward model can, though it can still be gamed. The GRPO and RLVR course covers this stage.

blocks.title: Post-training recipes compared

scenes.caption: InstructGPT (2022): one pass of SFT, reward model, then PPO with a KL penalty and pretraining mix.
Llama 2-Chat (2023): SFT, then iterated RLHF versions V1 to V5 with fresh preference data each time: rejection sampling alone until V4, then PPO applied on top of a rejection-sampled checkpoint.
Llama 3 (2024): six rounds, each with a reward model, rejection-sampled SFT data, SFT, then DPO instead of PPO. Simplified: rounds drawn as equal-length blocks.

DeepSeek-R1 (2025): cold-start SFT, RL with GRPO and rule-based rewards on reasoning tasks, rejection sampling plus SFT on broader data, then RL again with rule rewards and reward models. Simplified: stage lengths not to scale.

blocks.md: Whatever the algorithm, the ingredients are the same three: a strong pretrained model, a small set of high-quality demonstrations, and preference data with a mechanism (PPO, rejection sampling, DPO or RL against a checker) that moves the model toward preferred answers while staying near a reference.

blocks.question: In the toy, which beta gives the best true quality among the ones shown, and why is the smallest beta not best?
options: beta = 1, because past it the policy shifts mass to the response the reward model overrates
beta = 0.1, because it has the highest reward model score
beta = 100, because any change from SFT hurts
All are equal, because the reward model is unbiased on average
blocks.explain: True quality is 0.27 at beta = 1 versus 0.24 at 0.5 and -0.38 at 0.1. Small beta lets the policy concentrate on Flattery, which the reward model overrates. Some optimization helps: beta = 100 leaves quality at 0.10.

blocks.question: Best-of-N with N = 64 moves the output distribution how far from the base policy, by the analytic formula?
options: About 0.98 nats
About 4.16 nats
About 3.18 nats
About 64 nats
blocks.explain: log 64 - 63/64 = 4.159 - 0.984 = 3.175 nats. KL grows only logarithmically in N, which is why best-of-N is a gentle form of optimization.
